A viral video showing a group of men dancing to loud music inside a cave in Dehradun has drawn sharp criticism online, with users calling out what they described as a lack of civic sense at a shared tourist spot.The clip, shared on X by an account named @himalayanhindu, was reportedly filmed at Gucchu Paani in Uttarakhand’s capital. And when they get beaten start crying about how people discriminate them,” the user wrote.Another criticised not only the people seen in the video but also those supporting their behaviour online. “Zero civic sense in people in this video and people defending this in the comments,” the user wrote.No police action has been reported so far, and there has been no official word from local authorities on the video.

Article Title: Microsoft AI's chief marketing officer, Andra Mallard, is leaving the company, just 6 months after she joined; read email to employees
Article Text:

A shift in Microsoft's AI marketing strategy

Part of a broader reshuffle at Microsoft AI

What she worked on during her short tenure

Microsoft has confirmed that Andra Mallard, chief marketing officer of its AI unit, is leaving the company just six months after joining from Pinterest. According to a memo, viewed by Business Insider, Microsoft executive Yusuf Mehdi told employees that Mallard plans to relocate her family to Europe in August to be closer to her ailing father, leading her to step back from her role. Microsoft confirmed Mallard's departure plans, noting she will remain with the company until early next year in an advisory capacity. In the memo, Mehdi expressed appreciation for the energy and consumer-focused approach Mallard brought to accelerating Microsoft's Copilot marketing efforts, crediting her with helping push a more unified strategy, including the push toward a single app experience.“I’m grateful for the incredible energy and consumer‑centric ethos she’s brought to turbo‑charging our Copilot marketing efforts; Andrea has played a key role in advocating for a more unified approach, including the single app experience.”According to two people familiar with the matter, Mallard's exit also reflects a broader strategic shift underway at Microsoft AI as the company reconsiders its approach to consumer marketing. Microsoft is in the process of merging its separate consumer and business Copilot apps into a single unified application. Copilot, the company's flagship generative AI product, has generally trailed behind rival AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude in consumer adoption.Going forward, Copilot marketing responsibilities are being consolidated under Microsoft executive Jared Spataro, and the company does not plan to directly replace Mallard's CMO role.Mallard's departure comes amid a period of broader change within Microsoft AI, the unit where she had been hired as CMO. In March, Microsoft moved Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman into a new role focused on a superintelligence-focused team, while also consolidating its various commercial and consumer Copilot teams under new leadership.Mallard brought significant consumer marketing experience to the role. She spent more than seven years as Pinterest's chief marketing officer before joining Microsoft, and prior to that, led marketing at Gap's athleisure brand Athleta and served as CMO at virtual care company Omada Health.During her brief time at Microsoft, marketing initiatives included a Super Bowl advertisement showing NFL teams using Copilot in Excel to analyze athlete performance data and build scouting profiles of top prospects. Microsoft also worked with influencers such as Alix Earle, who has posted content featuring Copilot on her social media channels. Both of these projects, however, had begun before Mallard joined the company.
Article Summary: Andra Mallard, Microsoft's chief marketing officer of its AI unit, is leaving the company. Mallard will relocate her family to Europe in August to be closer to her ailing father. Her departure comes amid a period of broader change within Microsoft AI, the unit where she had been hired.

Article Title: Google and OpenAI are betting big on students, but why the risks are just as big
Article Text:
Disclaimer: It is an AI-generated image used for representative purpose only

Catch them young, keep them longer

But, becoming the homework machine carries risks

Then there is the much thornier and obvious question of safety

Feature ChatGPT Go Google Gemini Student Plan Pricing Rs 399/month (after free tier) Free for 1 year (Google AI Plus), then Rs 399/month Core AI Access GPT‑5.6 Luna with unlimited text chats Gemini Omni with 2× higher usage limits Study Tools Study mode with step‑by‑step guidance, practice questions Student hub with study notebooks, diagnostic quizzes, tailored study plans File & Image Support More uploads, larger documents, more image creation 400 GB cloud storage, integration with Google Drive, Lens, and Search Memory & Context Longer memory, extended context window Deep Research reports in Gemini Live, personalized learning Extra Benefits Voice chats, image generation, web search, instant insights Discounted bundle: Google AI Pro + YouTube Premium (up to 70% off) Availability Select regions Over 140 markets (excluding U.S., Canada, Hong Kong, etc.) Verification Standard subscription Student verification via SheerID required

The biggest AI companies have spent the past few years fighting for office workers, coders and consumers. Their next battleground may be far more consequential: the classroom. Google this week rolled out a clutch of new learning features across Search and Gemini, including customised quizzes, interactive visualisations, study notebooks and 3D simulations. Students can upload class notes, PDFs and slides and have AI turn them into study material. Gemini is also getting a dedicated Student Hub. Google has also announced 'Back to College' offer, that gives one year of Google AI Plus at no cost to eligible college students across India. The benefits include free access to Gemini Omni, 2x higher usage limits in Gemini, 400GB of storage, and more. Students can also avail a bundle of Google AI Pro and YouTube Premium at up to 70% discount.OpenAI, meanwhile, has launched ChatGPT for Teens, aimed at users aged 13-17. Along with tighter safety controls, the product includes Study Mode, quizzes and prompts designed to stop students from simply asking the chatbot to complete their homework. Last year, the company launched ChatGPT Go at Rs 300 per month. The plan offers unlimited text chats with GPT-5.6 Luna and few other benefits.Coming back to Google and OpenAI tapping students, the timing can be seen as hardly accidental.Students are already using AI. The companies are now trying to make sure they use their AI. Research by Pew earlier this year found that 54% of US teenagers had used chatbots for schoolwork and 57% had used them to search for information. A Common Sense Media study found that 67% of children aged 9-17 had used AI chatbots, with ChatGPT the most frequently mentioned service.There is a familiar Silicon Valley logic at work here: Habits formed early can be extremely difficult to break. Google became synonymous with internet search partly because an entire generation grew up “Googling” things. Microsoft spent decades pushing Office into schools and universities, knowing that students familiar with Word, Excel and PowerPoint would eventually carry those habits into workplaces.AI companies now have a similar opportunity. A student who uses Gemini to revise for an exam today could use it to write reports, analyse spreadsheets or prepare presentations when entering the workforce. A teenager accustomed to asking ChatGPT for explanations may eventually turn to it for coding, research, travel, financial information or work.That makes education strategically valuable even if teenagers themselves are not particularly lucrative customers. Google has already been courting college students with free access to paid Gemini features, while both Google and OpenAI are building products for schools and teachers alongside their student offerings.The prize, therefore, isn't merely subscription revenue from students. It is becoming the default AI interface for a generation. And there is another advantage. Education gives generative AI companies something they badly need: a use case that can be explained easily.“Ask AI anything” can sound vague. “Use AI to prepare for tomorrow's chemistry exam” does not. Quizzes, flashcards, personalised explanations and step-by-step tutoring are tangible applications that showcase exactly why somebody might want an AI assistant in the first place.There is an obvious problem with this strategy: AI can make completing schoolwork easier without necessarily making students better at learning. That distinction explains why both Google and OpenAI increasingly describe their products as tutors rather than answer machines.OpenAI's Study Mode is explicitly designed to take students through problems using questions and step-by-step guidance instead of immediately producing an answer. Its teen product can also detect when a user appears to be trying to shortcut homework and encourage them to use Study Mode instead.Google is following much the same route, surrounding Gemini with quizzes, interactive exercises and learning tools rather than simply improving its ability to spit out answers. That shift matters because schools are still grappling with plagiarism and AI-assisted cheating. Around six in ten US teens surveyed by Pew said students at their schools use AI chatbots to cheat at least sometimes.AI assistants are unusually intimate technology. Unlike a search engine, a chatbot holds conversations, remembers context and can appear remarkably human. Pew found that 12% of teens had already used chatbots for emotional support or advice.OpenAI's new teen experience consequently places stronger restrictions around self-harm, sexual content and other sensitive subjects, while adding parental controls and age estimation. The launch comes amid intense scrutiny of chatbot safety and litigation involving interactions between AI systems and minors.For AI companies, that creates an unusual trade-off. Teenagers may be among their most valuable long-term users, but they are also among the users requiring the strongest protections.Will the strategy pay off? Almost certainly in terms of adoption. AI has already entered classrooms regardless of whether schools formally embrace it. Turning that behaviour into structured learning products is more sensible than pretending students will stop using chatbots.The bigger uncertainty is whether today's winners will retain those users. Switching between AI assistants is far easier than moving between operating systems or social networks. There is little stopping a student from using Gemini for research, ChatGPT for explanations and another model for coding.So the race isn't merely to get students using AI first. It is to become the AI they instinctively open first.
Article Summary: Google and OpenAI launch ChatGPT for Teens, aimed at users aged 13-17. The product includes Study Mode, quizzes and prompts designed to stop students from simply asking the chatbot to complete their homework. Google has also announced 'Back to College' offer, that gives one year of Google AI Plus at no cost to eligible college students.

Article Title: Steve Jobs’ 8th-grade science project becomes an auction sensation as bids reached $8,475
Article Text:
Image: Left/RR Auction/Right/AI Genera​ted

From Steve Jobs’ school science fair project to a sought-after piece of Apple history

The project stayed with the Jobs family for decades

Bidding has pushed the project into five figures of interest

Other Apple memorabilia is also drawing big bids

A glimpse of the inventor before Apple

Long before Steve Jobs helped build Apple into one of the world’s most influential technology companies, he was already experimenting with electronics. A science project Jobs created while he was in eighth grade has now resurfaced decades later, offering collectors a rare glimpse into his early interest in technology. The project, titled “What is the Silicon-Controlled Rectifier?”, is part of an auction of Steve Jobs and Apple memorabilia marking Apple’s 50th anniversary. The collection includes vintage computers, signed documents, advertising material and other objects connected to Jobs and Apple’s early history. The school project reflects the hands-on curiosity that would later become a defining part of Jobs’ approach to technology and design.The project dates to February 29, 1968, when Jobs was an eighth-grade student. Rather than producing a conventional school display, he chose to explore the silicon-controlled rectifier, or SCR, a semiconductor device used to control electrical power. The surviving project consists of a large tri-fold display explaining the technology, along with demonstration circuits designed to show how the component worked.It also includes a written report and circuit diagrams created by Jobs. The project offers an unusually personal connection to Jobs because it predates the formation of Apple by several years. At the time, he was still a school student experimenting with electronics, long before he became associated with the development of personal computing. One small detail makes the project even more distinctive. Jobs left instructions for the science fair judges explaining how to use the circuits and reminding them to unplug the equipment afterwards. The warning suggests that the young Jobs was already paying close attention to how his technical work should be handled.Unlike many school projects that disappear after a science fair ends, this one remained within Jobs’ family for decades. According to a report by AppleInsider, the project comes from the personal collection of Jobs’ stepbrother, John Chovanec. It had remained at the Jobs family home in Los Altos before eventually becoming part of Chovanec’s collection. That provenance adds another layer of significance for collectors. The object is not simply an old electronics project associated with a famous person; it is a physical artefact from Jobs’ childhood that survived for more than half a century. Its survival also provides a rare look at Jobs before Apple existed. Much of the memorabilia associated with him comes from his professional career, particularly Apple’s early years. This project instead captures a much earlier stage of his life, when his interest in electronics was still developing.The science project is being sold as part of RR Auction’s “Steve Jobs & the Computer Revolution: The Apple 50th Anniversary Auction Part Two”. The auction contains more than 200 lots connected to Jobs, Apple and the history of personal computing. By August 19, bidding on the science project had reached $8,475, with the auction scheduled to close on August 20 at 6 p.m. Eastern Time. The auction house expects the project could ultimately sell for more than $20,000. The rising price reflects the unusual combination of technological history, personal provenance and Jobs’ connection to the object. A school science project might normally have little monetary value, but this one has become a piece of the story behind one of the world's most recognisable technology companies.The science project is only one part of the auction. Other lots offer collectors objects from different stages of Apple’s development, including vintage computers, components, advertising material and documents connected to Jobs. Among the more valuable items is an Apple-1 computer housed inside a Smith-Corona typewriter case. A Steve Jobs-signed Apple business card is also included, alongside other early Apple material. The auction follows an earlier sale that demonstrated just how much collectors are willing to pay for important pieces of Apple history. In the first part of the anniversary auction, the first cheque issued by Apple sold for $2.4 million, while an Apple-1 prototype board reached $2.75 million. Against those multimillion-dollar sales, Jobs’ eighth-grade project is a much smaller artefact. Yet its appeal comes from something those later objects cannot provide, it shows the future Apple co-founder before Apple existed.The value of Jobs’ science project ultimately goes beyond the electronics mounted on its wooden display. It captures an early moment in the life of someone who would later have an enormous influence on personal technology. The project does not show the finished products, dramatic launches or corporate milestones that later defined Jobs’ career. Instead, it shows a schoolboy investigating how a semiconductor worked and building a practical demonstration around it. That makes the object particularly compelling as Apple reaches its 50th anniversary. The company’s history is usually told through the Apple-1, Macintosh, iPod, iPhone and other landmark products. This small eighth-grade project offers a much earlier chapter, a physical reminder that the story of Jobs’ technological curiosity began long before the Apple logo became globally recognised. What began as an eighth-grade science experiment has now become a rare piece of technology history, with collectors bidding for a glimpse of Steve Jobs before he became Steve Jobs.
Article Summary: The project dates to February 29, 1968, when Jobs was an eighth-grade student. It is part of an auction of Steve Jobs and Apple memorabilia marking Apple’s 50th anniversary. By August 19, bidding on the science project had reached $8,475, with the auction scheduled to close on August 20 at 6 p.m. Eastern Time.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

The Nashik-Trimbakeshwar Kumbh Mela Authority (NTKMA) will deploy an AI-powered “Digital Twin” platform for crowd control, mobility planning, emergency response, and disaster preparedness at the Simhastha Kumbh Mela 2027, strengthening technology-led event management.The proposed system will create a live digital replica of the Kumbh ecosystem by integrating GIS-based 2D and 3D maps with real-time operational data, surveillance feeds and AI analytics. Officials said the platform would serve as a decision-support tool, enabling authorities to monitor ground conditions, assess risks and coordinate multiple agencies involved in managing the event.Built on Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC), ‘Digital Twin’ will function as a unified dashboard for departments handling crowd management, traffic, sanitation, health services, security, disaster management and public amenities. “The platform will continuously process data from multiple sources to provide a real-time view of the Kumbh environment. Authorities will be able to track crowd density, analyse movement patterns, generate alerts and assess operational challenges as they emerge. It will also allow officials to simulate scenarios and evaluate response strategies before implementation,” an official said.Crowd intelligence and public safety are expected to be among its key applications.“By analysing pedestrian movement and crowd concentrations across bathing ghats, temples, roads and transit hubs, officials will be able to identify bottlenecks and prevent congestion during peak pilgrimage days,” the official said.It will also support transport planning by integrating traffic flows, public transport operations, parking facilities and pedestrian movement into a single digital framework. Officials said this would help improve diversion plans, optimise resource deployment and strengthen mobility management.Beyond crowd and traffic monitoring, 'Digital Twin’ will cover health services, emergency response, sanitation and waste management, utility services, environmental and river monitoring, weather-risk assessment and disaster preparedness. It will also assist in workforce deployment, lost-and-found operations and citizen support services.“The initiative is part of the proposed Maha Simhastha Kumbh AI Stack, which also includes an AI-first call centre, AI-powered lost-and-found services and ‘KumbhDoot’, an AI-based virtual assistant for pilgrims,” another official said.The digital ecosystem is proposed to be integrated with the Kumbh website and mobile application, offering crowd-density heat maps, route guidance, SOS support, weather alerts, traffic updates, parking information and public facility details.NTKMA commissioner Shekhar Singh said 'Digital Twin’ would operate on a “human-in-the-loop” model, with AI-generated insights supporting rather than replacing administrative decision-making. “It will operate on a human-in-the-loop model, with intelligent automation complemented by human oversight and validation. Article Title: Blind photographers bring their world to life at IIT-M exhibition
Article Text:
New perspectives

Chennai:





A beam of sunlight falling on a patch of dead leaves. A cat sunning herself. A canopy of trees. At a glance, they would seem like regular photographs, but these are different. All the 50 pictures on display at the exhibition at IIT Madras this week were clicked by blind photographers aided by sighted co-creators.The group of photographers, mostly comprising colleges students from across the country, attended a three-day workshop at IIT-M, where they worked with co-creators from the department of media studies at SRM.“It had just rained, and my co-creator told me the weather was beautiful. I balanced the phone against my head and captured the sunshine coming through the branches along with a hint of rain, and it came out beautifully,” says Hemachandran Karah, one of the participants, who is also an assistant professor at IIT-M and the co-founder and head of The Accessibility Research Centre. “Visually impaired people have to use our own body as tripod—we hold the phone or camera against our chest, forehead, etc,” he adds.Another of his clicks is one of an electric buggy—he measured its width using footsteps and then stepped back to get a wide angle. “We get the help of AI on our phones, which says what the image is. But even before AI, visually impaired people were taking photographs using their sense of touch and smell,” says Hemachandran.“I felt the leaves with my hands and wanted to photograph them,” says Karthikayeni G, another participant. “During the workshop, the instructors had taught us when to use landscape and portrait modes. I sought the help of my co-creator for that and clicked the photo, and everyone said it came out well,” she says. “All the photos have a QR code which opens to an explanation of what the photo is about. I hope this facility is introduced in all govt and public exhibitions so that the visually challenged can also experience them. ”The exhibition is on at Alliance Francaise till Aug 26.
Article Summary: All the 50 pictures on display at the exhibition at IIT Madras this week were clicked by blind photographers aided by sighted co-creators. “We get the help of AI on our phones, which says what the image is,” says Hemachandran Karah, one of the participants.

Article Title: Part-time online job scam: Senior citizen duped of Rs 24.93 lakh in Tamil Nadu
Article Text: COIMBATORE: A 62-year-old man in Coimbatore district was cheated of Rs 24.93 lakh in a part-time online job scam.According to police, V Subburaj, 62, of Pollachi received an advertisement on the Telegram messaging app offering a part-time job involving hotel booking and writing reviews on hotels. A cyber fraudster, using the Telegram handle @Miaaaana577, enticed Subburaj to create user IDs on malicious sites (including hotings.vip and httngt.com) and complete assigned tasks.The fraudster promised lucrative profit margins and instructed Subburaj to make a deposit to assign him tasks. He also promised that once the task was complete, the deposit amount along with the profit would be transferred. Believing this, he transferred a total sum of Rs 24,93,940 in 41 online transactions into various suspect bank accounts provided by the fraudsters.When he attempted to withdraw his earned profit, the scammers demanded an additional “tax payment.” Realising he had been duped, the man lodged a complaint with the district cybercrime police on Wednesday.Based on the complaint, police registered a case under sections 318(4) and 319(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and Section 66(D) of the Information Technology (IT) Act, and started an investigation.

V Subburaj, 62, of Pollachi received an advertisement on the Telegram messaging app offering a job. Article Title: In 2017, Germany’s Freiburg opened a city hall with solar-powered walls designed to produce more energy than the building needs
Article Text:
Image: World Green Building Council

Freiburg’s newest town hall was designed as an energy-producing building

Freiburg’s newest town hall was designed as an energy-producing building (Image: AI Generated)

Solar panels cover the parts of the building exposed to sunlight

Its insulation and ventilation systems help keep energy demand low

The building produces more electricity than it needs

Freiburg turned everyday government architecture into a renewable-energy showcase

A city hall where the building can give electricity back

In Freiburg, south-west Germany, a city hall has been designed to do something unusual for a government building: produce more energy than it consumes. Completed in 2017, the city’s latest town hall combines high-performance solar panels with an energy-efficient design that sharply reduces the building’s demand for heating, cooling, ventilation and lighting. The World Green Building Council lists City Hall Freiburg at Fehrenbachallee and describes it as a surplus-energy building, noting that photovoltaic units on the roof and sun-exposed parts of the façade generate more electricity than the building requires. The project goes beyond simply adding solar panels to an existing office. Its insulation, ventilation, heating and cooling systems were designed together as part of a wider energy concept. Freiburg’s official tourism site also notes that construction began in 2014 and that, after completion in 2017, the building was expected to generate more energy than it needed.The building is located at Fehrenbachallee in Freiburg, Baden-Württemberg, rather than at the historic Rathausplatz associated with Freiburg’s older town halls. The World Green Building Council identifies its construction/refurbishment date as 2017 and records its address as Fehrenbachallee, Freiburg, Baden-Württemberg 79106, Germany.That distinction is useful because Freiburg has several buildings referred to as town halls. The city’s official tourism website explains that the latest town hall was constructed between 2014 and 2017, while the older New Town Hall is a much earlier Renaissance complex. The modern building was therefore created specifically for contemporary administration, with energy performance incorporated into its architecture from the beginning. Rather than treating electricity generation as an addition, its designers made renewable energy and low consumption central to the building's operation.One of the most distinctive elements of the project is the way photovoltaic technology has been incorporated into both the roof and façade. The roof and areas of the façade exposed to direct sunlight are fitted with high-performance solar energy panels. These panels have a dual function: they generate electricity while also shielding parts of the building from direct solar radiation. That approach makes the building itself part of its energy infrastructure. Instead of requiring a separate solar farm or relying entirely on rooftop space, the architecture provides additional surfaces for electricity generation. The strategy is particularly relevant in urban areas, where land can be expensive and limited. Freiburg’s latest town hall demonstrates how walls and roofs that would normally serve only structural or protective purposes can also contribute to a building’s energy supply. The result is a structure where renewable-energy production is visible in the architecture rather than hidden away.Producing large quantities of solar electricity is only half of the building’s energy strategy. Freiburg’s town hall was also designed to need less energy in the first place. The building has outstanding thermal insulation that permits low-temperature heating and high-temperature cooling. Its ventilation system incorporates heat recovery, reducing the amount of energy lost through the movement of indoor and outdoor air. The building also uses groundwater as part of its heating and cooling strategy. A heat pump operates the heating system, while a plate heat exchanger provides cooling. These systems work alongside the building envelope and ventilation system rather than functioning as isolated technologies. This integrated approach is important because an energy-positive building cannot depend solely on generating more electricity. Its performance also depends on controlling how much energy is required to maintain comfortable conditions for the people working inside.The combination of low energy demand and substantial photovoltaic generation gives Freiburg’s town hall its defining characteristic. The World Green Building Council describes it as Europe’s biggest surplus-energy building and says its photovoltaic units produce more electricity than the building needs. The surplus does not simply disappear. The building can respond to requirements from the electricity network and feed excess electricity back into the grid. This means the town hall can function not only as an energy consumer but also as a small-scale producer contributing electricity beyond its own immediate needs. The concept changes the traditional relationship between buildings and power systems. Instead of a building continuously drawing electricity from an external network, the building can generate renewable power, satisfy its own requirements and return excess generation to the wider system.The project is particularly striking because it applies advanced energy principles to an ordinary civic function. A city hall is primarily a workplace for public administration, yet Freiburg’s building has been designed to demonstrate what that workplace can achieve environmentally. The project is recorded under its net-zero operational carbon category and holds a DGNB Climate Positive certification. Freiburg's official tourism information places the project within the city's broader collection of town halls, but the 2017 building represents a sharp contrast with the historic structures. The older buildings reflect centuries of civic and architectural history; the latest one reflects a contemporary attempt to reduce the environmental cost of running a large public building. Its significance therefore lies not simply in the number of solar panels installed, but in how architecture, insulation, ventilation, heating, cooling and renewable generation were brought together into one energy concept.Freiburg’s modern town hall demonstrates a different way of thinking about public buildings. Instead of designing a structure that simply consumes energy and then adding solar panels afterwards, the project combines low demand, renewable generation and energy-efficient systems from the outset. The building generates more energy than it requires for heating, cooling, ventilation and lighting, with surplus electricity capable of being fed into the grid. That makes the building more than an administrative workplace. Its roof and sun-facing façade generate power, its insulation reduces energy loss, its ventilation system recovers heat, and its heating and cooling systems make use of groundwater. Together, these features turn Freiburg’s town hall into a practical demonstration of how public architecture can contribute to the energy transition. Rather than merely occupying space within a city, the building actively produces some of the energy that the city and its occupants depend upon.
Article Summary: Freiburg’s newest town hall was designed as an energy-producing building. Solar panels on the roof and sun-exposed parts of the façade generate more electricity than the building requires. insulation, ventilation, heating and cooling systems were designed together as part of a wider energy concept.

Article Title: China’s 16.18-km undersea high-speed rail tunnel completes 21-day cutter replacement under extreme pressure
Article Text:
Image: AI Generated

How China’s Jintang undersea tunnel completed high-pressure shield cutter replacement

Engineers replaced 104 cutting tools under high pressure

The “Deep-Sea Space Station” allows longer work shifts

China is pushing high-speed rail through underwater environments

Deep beneath the waters off eastern China, engineers are carrying out one of the most demanding stages of construction on a high-speed railway tunnel. The Jintang undersea tunnel, part of the Ningbo-Zhoushan high-speed railway in Zhejiang Province, has completed the inspection and replacement of 104 shield cutting tools after 21 days of work under intense water and soil pressure. The 16.18-kilometre tunnel is set to become the world’s longest undersea high-speed rail tunnel, linking Ningbo with Zhoushan and cutting the journey between the two cities from as much as two hours to about 26 minutes. The latest operation also tested a domestically developed saturation hyperbaric system adapted from deep-sea diving technology. The achievement comes as China continues pushing high-speed rail construction through challenging underwater environments, including the recently completed shield-machine crossing beneath the Yangtze River, another major engineering milestone highlighted by China’s State Council Information Office . The operation demonstrates how construction methods are being adapted to underwater conditions safely too.The Jintang tunnel is the critical undersea section of the Ningbo-Zhoushan high-speed railway and stretches 16.18 kilometres, including an 11.21-kilometre shield-bored section. It will connect the port city of Ningbo with the Zhoushan islands, where journeys currently rely heavily on roads and ferries. Once the railway opens, travel between Ningbo and Zhoushan is expected to take as little as 26 minutes, compared with roughly 1.5 to 2 hours today.The tunnel is being excavated from opposite shores using two super-large-diameter shield machines. One machine, Yongzhou, must bore 4,940 metres through 24 alternating layers of soft and hard rock, representing nearly 70 per cent of its route and creating severe wear on its cutting tools. Excavation progress is being monitored carefully. The geological conditions make the project particularly demanding. Rock strength along the route reaches 191 megapascals, placing some of the material in the high-strength to very-high-strength category. As the cutting head moves through alternating rock layers, its tools experience substantial mechanical stress and wear. That made the latest replacement operation necessary, but carrying out such maintenance deep beneath the seabed presented a challenge of its own. At the tunnel’s deepest point, the excavation reaches about 92 metres below sea level, where combined water and soil pressure can reach 8.5 bar. A roughly 2,000-metre section experiences pressure above 6 bar. These conditions mean that workers cannot simply enter the cutting chamber using conventional methods and carry out maintenance as they would in a normal tunnel.The latest operation involved inspecting and replacing 104 shield cutting tools over 21 days. These tools sit at the front of the tunnel-boring machine and are responsible for breaking through the rock and soil ahead of it. Their condition is critical because worn cutters can reduce excavation efficiency and make continued tunnelling more difficult. The operation was carried out under high water pressure, turning what would ordinarily be a demanding mechanical maintenance job into a complex human-safety challenge. Global Times reported that conventional compressed-air methods provide workers with only around 40 minutes of effective working time per person each day and are generally limited to depths of approximately 60 metres. The Jintang tunnel’s deeper and higher-pressure conditions required a different approach. The construction team spent three years adapting technology derived from deep-sea saturation diving. The result was described as China’s first domestically developed saturation hyperbaric system for shield tunnelling, nicknamed the “Deep-Sea Space Station” by the project team. Rather than repeatedly exposing workers to major pressure changes, the system allows them to remain in a controlled pressurised environment for extended periods.The system consists of living, transfer and control modules designed to allow workers to operate safely under the extreme conditions surrounding the tunnel boring machine. The system can accommodate nine workers for extended periods, with crew members travelling to the work face through a transfer chamber. They can work for up to eight hours at a time, allowing round-the-clock multi-shift operations for as long as 28 days. One of the key advantages is that workers undergo a single controlled decompression after completing their assignment instead of repeatedly moving between normal atmospheric pressure and the high-pressure working environment. This reduces the risks associated with frequent pressure changes and makes prolonged underwater construction work more manageable. The technology represents an unusual overlap between offshore engineering and underground construction. Techniques developed for people working at significant depths underwater have been adapted to create a controlled environment inside a tunnel-boring operation. In practical terms, the system gives engineers more time at the cutting face while reducing the number of dangerous pressure transitions workers must endure. The successful 21-day cutter replacement operation therefore represents more than routine maintenance. It provided a real-world test of whether the new system could support prolonged work under the pressure conditions encountered by the Jintang tunnel.The Jintang project forms part of a broader expansion of high-speed rail infrastructure through some of China’s most challenging terrain. The Ningbo-Zhoushan railway is designed to bring Zhoushan more directly into the national high-speed rail network, with the undersea tunnel providing a crucial connection beneath the water separating the islands from mainland Zhejiang. The project also comes shortly after another major underwater railway milestone in China. On July 31, 2026, the State Council Information Office reported that China had completed excavation of the tunnel beneath the Yangtze River for the Shanghai-Chongqing-Chengdu high-speed railway. The project uses the large-diameter shield machine Linghang and is designed for high-speed trains travelling at up to 350 kilometres per hour without slowing for the underwater section.The two projects involve different waterways and engineering challenges, but together they demonstrate the scale of China’s efforts to extend high-speed rail through difficult underwater environments. While the Yangtze project required a record-setting shield machine to pass beneath one of the country’s largest rivers, the Jintang project is tackling prolonged excavation beneath the seabed, where high rock strength and intense pressure complicate both boring and maintenance. For the Jintang tunnel, is also another step towards completing a connection expected to dramatically shorten travel between Ningbo and Zhoushan. The Yongzhou shield machine has already advanced 3,936 metres, or nearly 80 per cent of its assigned task. If construction continues as planned, the finished tunnel will not simply provide a faster route between two cities. It will also stand as a demonstration of how large-scale rail infrastructure can be built in environments where conventional tunnelling techniques reach their limits, with workers and machines operating beneath some of the most challenging pressure conditions encountered in modern rail construction.
Article Summary: Engineers replaced 104 cutting tools under high pressure. The Jintang undersea tunnel is part of the Ningbo-Zhoushan high-speed railway in Zhejiang Province. The 16.18-kilometre tunnel is set to become the world’s longest undersea high- speed rail tunnel.

Article Title: Archaeologists find earliest physical evidence of brass-making in East Asia in southern China
Article Text:
Archaeologists find the earliest physical evidence of brass-making in East Asia in southern China (PC: Cambridge University Press)

Ancient crucibles reveal early brass-making in medieval China

Ancient crucibles reveal early brass-making in medieval China (PC: AI Generated)

How did ancient craftspeople make brass from copper and zinc

How did brass-making technology reach medieval Guangzhou

What does the discovery reveal about medieval metallurgy in China

A set of ancient crucibles found in Guangzhou is giving archaeologists new clues about how brass-making technology may have reached medieval China. The vessels came from an official metallurgical workshop at the Royal Palace of the Nanyue Kingdom and dated from the ninth and tenth centuries AD. Their metal residues show that craftspeople were producing brass locally through cementation rather than simply working with imported objects. According to a research article published by Cambridge University Press, titled ‘ Brass technology transmission via maritime routes: crucible evidence from southern China ’, points towards wider technological connections with the Islamic world. Guangzhou was a major trading port, and the authors suggest maritime routes may have helped move metallurgical knowledge across regions. The study analysed crucibles using chemical, microscopic and lead-isotope methods. Together, the findings provide direct archaeological evidence for medieval brass production in southern China and offer clues about how the technology may have travelled.Archaeologists found three well-preserved brass-making crucibles at an official metallurgical workshop in Guangzhou. The workshop was part of the Royal Palace of the Nanyue Kingdom site and was active across many centuries.The three crucibles belong to the ninth–tenth century group. Each was cup-shaped with a slightly inward-sloping rim and a rounded base. Some had a pouring spout. They measured about 60-80 mm across and 60-70 mm high, with a capacity of roughly 0.2-0.3 litres. Researchers found heavy heat damage and glassy material on their surfaces. Metal residues inside included copper, zinc compounds and brass droplets. A nearby semi-subterranean furnace also dates to the seventh-tenth centuries. Together, these remains provide direct evidence of metalworking at the site.The crucial evidence came from residues left inside the crucibles. Microscopic and chemical analyses identified zinc oxide, zinc silicate, and droplets of brass. One group of crucibles contained high-purity copper and binary brass droplets with about 11-17% zinc. Another contained bronze with tin alongside zinc and produced a copper-zinc-tin alloy. The researchers interpret these residues as evidence for cementation. In this process, zinc-bearing material is heated with copper or a copper alloy so zinc enters the metal and forms brass. The remains therefore show more than the presence of finished brass objects. They preserve traces of the production process itself.The study also examined lead isotopes to investigate the likely origin of the raw materials. The three analysed crucibles had similar lead-isotope ratios that fit signatures associated with the Cathaysia tectonic province. Because these signatures occur widely across southern China, the researchers say a local source for the raw materials is reasonable. The technology itself may have travelled from farther west. The authors point to similarities between the Guangzhou crucibles and brass-making vessels associated with the Islamic world. Guangzhou was also a major international trading port. Historical evidence records connections between the city and Arab merchants. The researchers therefore suggest that maritime routes and the movement of merchants and craftsmen may have helped transmit brass-making knowledge to southern China.The findings add important evidence to the history of brass production in China. Local brass production is generally thought to have begun around the tenth century AD, but the Guangzhou crucibles provide direct evidence from the ninth-tenth centuries. The researchers argue that the discovery helps explain how a specialised metallurgical technique became established locally. It also shows why archaeological workshops can reveal details that written records alone cannot provide. The study does not claim that every element of brass technology came from one place or through one route. Instead, it highlights a possible connection between western technological traditions, maritime trade and local production in Guangzhou. The evidence adds an important piece to the history of metallurgy in East Asia.
Article Summary: Archaeologists found three well-preserved brass-making crucibles at an official metallurgical workshop in Guangzhou. The crucibles dated from the ninth and tenth centuries AD. Their metal residues show that craftspeople were producing brass locally through cementation rather than simply working with imported objects.

Article Title: Japan installed a 1.1 MW turbine beneath the Naru Strait, using predictable tidal currents to generate clean electricity for the Goto Islands
Article Text:
Image AI generated

How Japan’s 1.1 MW AR1100 tidal turbine generates electricity underwater

Image AI generated

Japan’s tidal energy project grows from a 500 kW pilot to a 1.1 MW turbine

Why predictable tidal energy could complement solar and wind in Japan

The engineering challenges of operating a tidal turbine underwater

Between Japan’s Goto Islands, the sea is doing something that is usually associated with wind farms and solar fields. Beneath the surface of the Naru Strait, a 1.1 MW turbine is drawing energy from water moving with the tides and sending electricity back towards land through a subsea cable. No blades are turning in the sky and no panels spread across the shoreline. The machine works largely out of sight, following currents whose timing can be forecast well in advance. Installed by Proteus Marine Renewables, the AR1100 grew from an earlier 500 kW trial in the same waters. Its deployment has given Japan a megawatt-scale tidal system designed to work with the regular rise and fall of the sea rather than depending on sunshine or changing winds.The project also demonstrates the potential of tidal power in narrow channels, where fast-moving water can provide a concentrated source of renewable energy. By placing the turbine underwater, the system avoids taking up large areas of land while tapping into a resource that follows a predictable natural cycle.The AR1100 is installed in the Naru Strait near Japan’s Goto Islands. Unlike a conventional wind turbine, there is no tower standing above the water and no set of panels covering land.The generating equipment works underwater, where tidal currents pass through its three-bladed rotor and turn the machinery inside the nacelle. Electricity then travels towards shore through a subsea connection. According to Proteus Marine Renewables, the turbine was deployed in February 2025, while later company information recorded that it received Japanese certification and began exporting electricity to the grid in June 2025.The arrangement is fairly straightforward in principle, although operating it beneath the sea is not. The rotor extracts energy from moving water, the drivetrain passes that mechanical power to a permanent-magnet generator, and the resulting electricity is carried to an onshore station. A yaw system turns the nacelle as the tidal flow reverses, while independently controlled blades can alter their pitch to regulate how the turbine responds to changing conditions. AR1100 is a horizontal-axis turbine mounted on a gravity-based support structure. The earlier project in the same strait provided the starting point for the larger machine.Offshore Energy reported that the earlier 500 kW AR500 pilot operated in the Naru Strait with 97% availability in 2021. That earlier machine had a rated capacity of 500 kW and recorded 97% availability during its operation, according to the material released about the project. The experience allowed engineers to see how the technology behaved in the actual marine environment rather than only in controlled testing.The next version increased the rated capacity to 1.1 MW and introduced changes to the turbine's control systems. An equipment supply and works contract with Kyuden Mirai Energy was signed in November 2022, with the Japanese project subsequently moving towards the upgraded machine. Advanced pitch and yaw systems were incorporated as part of the work. The company says those changes were intended to improve the turbine's performance and efficiency while allowing it to deal more effectively with the changing direction of the tidal flow.The most distinctive feature of tidal power is not simply that the turbines sit underwater. It is the predictability of the resource. Solar output changes with daylight and weather conditions. Wind can strengthen, weaken or stop altogether. ClickPetroleogas noted that tidal production can be estimated in advance because the cycles follow predictable natural patterns, unlike renewable generation that is more affected by weather conditions. The electricity produced at any particular moment still depends on the conditions at the site and the performance of the equipment; the underlying movement of the water is far less of a surprise.That distinction matters when renewable sources are being combined. A grid operator cannot make the sun shine or order the wind to blow, whereas the timing of tidal cycles can be incorporated into generation planning. It does not make tidal energy constant; the flow rises and falls as the tide changes, but it makes the pattern easier to anticipate. For islands such as those around the Goto group, where space and fuel logistics can present particular constraints, a submerged source can sit alongside solar, wind and other forms of generation. The Naru Strait project is intended to contribute to reducing emissions from the islands' electricity supply.Underwater generation creates its own engineering problems. Components have to survive saltwater, strong currents and long periods of exposure while remaining accessible enough for inspection and maintenance. Getting people and equipment to a submerged turbine can also require vessels, specialist crews and careful planning. The location itself has to provide sufficient water movement, suitable depth and a practical route for sending the electricity into the grid.The Naru Strait project therefore depends on more than the turbine turning. Its subsea cable links the machine to an onshore electrical station, where the generated power can be processed for distribution. Local vessels and resources were used during deployment, with Proteus' offshore team overseeing the work, while Kyuden Mirai Energy and Japan's Ministry of Environment have been involved in advancing the project.There is also a useful way to think about the long-term promise of the machine, without treating its output as something that can be guaranteed hour by hour. The tidal timetable itself is highly predictable. Engineers can calculate when stronger and weaker currents are expected well into the future, creating a generation pattern that can be plotted ahead of time. What cannot simply be printed on that chart is the turbine's actual electricity production for every future hour: maintenance, operating conditions and other technical factors still matter.That distinction is important. The Naru Strait turbine is not a giant power station, nor does the available source material establish that it will produce a fixed amount of electricity every hour for a decade. What the project demonstrates is something more specific: a megawatt-scale machine can be installed beneath a Japanese strait, connected to shore and operated using an energy source whose basic timing is known far in advance. The water will keep changing direction. The turbine is built to follow it.
Article Summary: The AR1100 is installed in the Naru Strait near Japan’s Goto Islands. Unlike a conventional wind turbine, there is no tower standing above the water and no set of panels covering land. The generating equipment works underwater, where tidal currents pass through its three-bladed rotor and turn the machinery inside the nacelle. Electricity then travels towards shore through a subsea connection.

Article Title: Ironmouse Fortnite crossover: Is Epic Games teasing a ‘skin’ after adding her new Sprite?
Article Text:
Ironmouse Fortnite crossover: Is Epic Games teasing a ‘skin’ after adding her new Sprite?

Ironmouse Fortnite Sprite arrives in v41.30 update

Will Ironmouse get a Fortnite skin?

Ironmouse, one of the most popular VTubers and streamers on Twitch, has officially become part of Fortnite, getting herself an in-game Sprite with the release of the Fortnite v41.30 patch on July 30, 2026. Article Title: Meet Rayhan Papar, the 18-year-old Texas student who trained a da Vinci surgical robot to remove tumors; it succeeded in 3 of 4 gel-model tests
Article Text:
Meet Rayhan Papar, the 18-year-old Texas student (Image Credit: Society for Science/Chris Ayers Photography)

Sim-to-Real for Autonomous Tumor Resection via Minimally Invasive Robotics

Teaching a robot to operate

From simulation to the da Vinci system

Why the research matters

Poll Vote & Share your view How important do you believe simulation training is for surgical robots? Very important Somewhat important Not important at all 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Surgical robots are already used in operating rooms around the world, helping surgeons perform complex procedures with remarkable precision. But these machines are still controlled by human surgeons. Now, an 18-year-old student from Texas has explored what it could take to teach a surgical robot to carry out one of the most delicate tasks in medicine: identifying and removing a tumour on its own.According to the Society for Science, Rayhan Papar, an 18-year-old student from Spring, Texas, developed a framework to help surgical robots learn autonomous tumour removal. His project, titled, was tested on a da Vinci surgical system and successfully removed whole tumours in three of four gel-model tests. Papar was also named a finalist in the Regeneron Science Talent Search 2026.The idea behind Papar's project was not to replace surgeons or create a robot ready to perform operations on patients. Instead, his work focused on one of the biggest challenges in surgical robotics: how to train a machine to deal with the unpredictable conditions found inside the human body.A surgical robot cannot simply follow the same set of instructions every time.Every patient's anatomy is different, and soft tissues can move, deform and change shape during a procedure. They also have to operate within a restricted visual field, while tissues can move and change size and shape during surgery. These factors make it difficult to train a robot to carry out a task independently.Papar's solution was to begin in a simulated environment rather than directly training the robot in the physical world. He created a physics-based simulation using medical imaging to reconstruct anatomy. Within this virtual environment, the robot could learn how to approach and remove a tumour while accounting for the physical behaviour of tissues and the constraints of minimally invasive surgery.In simple terms, the robot was first given an opportunity to learn and make decisions in a computer-generated surgical setting before those lessons were transferred to a real robotic system.This process is often described as a “sim-to-real” approach. The aim is to use simulation as a safer and more practical training ground before testing whether the robot's learned skills can work in the physical world. The framework was designed to bridge the gap between simulation and real-world robotic performance, allowing the system to apply its virtual learning to a physical robotic platform.The framework was then tested on a da Vinci surgical system, a robotic platform designed for minimally invasive surgery. In four gel-model tests, the system achieved complete tumour removal in three cases, according to the Society for Science.The gel models are an important detail. These were not human patients, and the results do not mean that an autonomous surgical robot is now ready for use in hospitals. Gel models provide a controlled experimental setting, allowing researchers to test a robotic system's performance before attempting more complex and clinically relevant studies. Still, achieving complete tumour removal in three of the four tests offers an early demonstration of how simulation-based training could help robots perform highly specialised surgical tasks.Surgical robots can offer precision and dexterity, particularly in procedures performed through small incisions. However, human surgeons remain responsible for operating these systems and making critical decisions during surgery. Research such as Papar's explores whether some parts of a surgical procedure could eventually become more autonomous. Before that could happen, however, robots would need to reliably understand changing anatomy, adapt to moving and deformable tissue, recognise surgical targets and respond safely when conditions do not match expectations.That is where the simulation component of Papar's work becomes significant. Training in a virtual environment could potentially allow robotic systems to encounter many different surgical scenarios before being tested in physical models. The project also highlights the growing intersection of robotics, computer science, medical imaging and surgery. Rather than treating a surgical robot as a machine that simply repeats programmed movements, the research explores how it might learn to make task-related decisions within a changing environment.Papar, who attends The Woodlands College Park High School, also holds a patent for a surgical aid designed to help with brain tumour resection, according to the Society for Science. Beyond his research, he mentors other students working on STEM projects and co-founded IdeaCharge, a nonprofit that teaches children about electrical engineering.His project is still an experimental research effort, and its results should be viewed in that context. A success rate of three out of four tests in gel models is an encouraging early result, not evidence that autonomous tumour-removal robots are ready for clinical use.However, the experiment offers a glimpse into a possible future direction for surgical robotics, one in which machines may be trained extensively in realistic simulations before helping surgeons perform increasingly complex tasks. For Papar, that future began with four gel-model tests, three successful tumour removals and a question that could shape the next generation of medical robotics: can a surgical robot learn not just to follow commands, but to make the right decisions when the surgical environment changes?
Article Summary: Rayhan Papar, an 18-year-old student from Spring, Texas, developed a framework to help surgical robots learn autonomous tumour removal. His project was tested on a da Vinci surgical system and successfully removed whole tumours in three of four gel-model tests. The framework was designed to bridge the gap between simulation and real-world robotic performance.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.
